# Mitacintijātaka (Ja 114)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mitacintijātaka* (Ja 114) is a short narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877]. Its frame story (*paccuppannavatthu*) is set at Jetavana, delivered by the Buddha concerning two elderly monks (*mahallakattherā*) who, after completing a rains retreat in a country forest, repeatedly postponed their journey to visit the Master month after month due to procrastination [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1877].
In the story of the past (*atītavatthu*), set during the reign of King Brahmadatta of Bārāṇasī, three fish lived in the river of Bārāṇasī: Bahucinti, Appacinti, and Mitacinti [Fausböll 1877]. When they drifted into human-inhabited waters, Mitacinti warned the other two that the area was perilous because fishermen set various nets and wicker traps, advising an immediate return to the safety of the wilderness; however, out of laziness and attachment to food, the two companions kept delaying their departure day by day for three months until a fisherman's net trapped them [Fausböll 1877]. In the conclusion (*samodhāna*), the Buddha explains that the two procrastinating fish were reborn as the two elderly monks, while Mitacinti was the Bodhisatta; at the close of the teaching, both monks attained stream-entry (*sotāpattiphala*) [Fausböll 1877].
In modern scholarship, the narrative has been examined in relation to animal *svabhāva* (innate nature) within Indian fable literature, such as the *Pañcatantra* and *Hitopadeśa* [Levitt 2009]. Parallels to the narrative of the three fish are found in the *Mahābhārata* and the *Pañcatantra* tradition, though the *Mitacintijātaka* shares no core verse with these other Indian recensions [Söhnen-Thieme]. Neither SuttaCentral nor DharmaNexus reports any internal canonical text reuse or cross-language Buddhist parallels, though SuttaCentral records translations into four modern languages [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus].
